My research connects molecular identification, population genetics,
genomics, and movement ecology to address questions relevant to marine
conservation and fisheries management.

## Population genetics for fisheries management

Reliable genetic baselines are essential for investigating population
structure and connectivity in exploited marine species.

During my PhD, I developed population-genetic baselines for marine
invertebrates and explored how this information could contribute to
sustainable fisheries management.

## Molecular reference resources for biodiversity monitoring

Molecular monitoring depends on reliable links between DNA sequences
and taxonomic identities.

During my first postdoctoral fellowship, I worked on integrative
taxonomic and DNA-barcoding resources for vulnerable marine ecosystems,
helping establish the reference information needed for future
environmental DNA (eDNA) monitoring.

## Linking genomic variation and movement in Atlantic cod

At Dalhousie University, I work on the Northern Cod Acoustic Tracking
(NCAT) project in Daniel Ruzzante’s laboratory.

I integrate low-coverage whole-genome sequencing (lcWGS) with acoustic
telemetry to investigate relationships between genomic variation and
individual movement patterns in Atlantic cod.

This work brings together population-genomic analyses, the management
of large sequencing datasets, and the interpretation of movement and
spatial connectivity data.

## A long-term perspective

Across these research areas, my goal is to strengthen the biological
evidence available for marine species with limited genomic resources.

By developing expertise in a comparatively data-rich system, I aim
to identify approaches that can ultimately be adapted to marine
invertebrates and other data-poor systems.
